docs.title: Physical and motor access
docs.text:
Players can rebind movement and fire through a keyboard/mouse Settings menu. Menu navigation remains fixed after rebinding. Gameplay input is released on focus loss and while Settings is open. Returning from Settings waits for keys to be released before gameplay resumes.

See controls and Settings.

Limitations: no controller support, toggle-to-fire mode or one-handed preset. Holding Fire is reported continuously; client/game systems own firing behavior.

docs.title: Audio and visual access
docs.text:
Settings provides volume, mute and text sizes of 100%, 125% and 150%. Audio failures leave input and rendering operational. Server game events trigger sound effects. No equivalent text or dedicated visual cue is currently provided when audio is muted or unavailable; this remains an accessibility limitation.

Player names supplement the colors of server-controlled ships. Names come from connection and player-joined messages; an unknown name displays Player. Connection statuses use explicit headings and messages instead of color or sound alone. They use light text on a dark background, wrap messages and truncate when the available vertical space is exhausted.

An optional scene tint offers red, green, blue or amber at adjustable opacity. This is a visual preference, not a validated color-vision correction. Essential information must remain identifiable without color.

Text-size settings apply to Settings, status pages and client-supplied scene and overlay text. Scene text follows world scaling; HUD positions remain in window pixels. Font size and spacing also follow the text-size preference. Client HUD layout must accommodate larger text.

Limitations: no screen-reader integration or localization. The built-in font has limited glyph coverage. Real window readability still requires manual checks, including 640 x 360 and large text.

docs.title: Mental and cognitive access
docs.text:
Settings uses labeled values, explicit Apply and save, Back and Restore defaults actions. Unapplied changes are discarded on Back, and saved settings are restored on later launches.

Background motion can be disabled independently of game simulation. Status pages are static and do not flash or dismiss themselves. When a status is supplied, it hides the game view to avoid showing stale positions.

Limitations: no tutorial, simplified difficulty setting or interactive reconnect screen. The GUI does not decide connection, retry, timeout or recovery rules.

docs.title: Supply status feedback
docs.text:
rtype::gui::RenderScene scene;
scene.feedback.status = rtype::gui::GuiStatus::Disconnected;
scene.feedback.message = "The server stopped responding.";
gui.render(scene);

Supported statuses are None, Connecting, Rejected, Disconnected and Error. An empty message selects a status-specific default. Status rendering uses the built-in font without custom assets. Supply None with a current scene when gameplay may resume.

Continue calling pollActions() on status pages so Settings remains usable. Rendering a status does not clear the client world or stop existing audio.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: See the Settings checklist. Automated checks cover settings, keyboard mapping, persistence, status layouts and tint drawing order. Physical rendering, audio and multiplayer integration require manual checks. No accessibility certification is claimed.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Keep it high level: subsystems and how they interact, not every class.

The GUI supplies actions to client coordination, which builds scenes and sound events from server state. Client and server network layers exchange UDP messages; gameplay decisions remain in the server simulation.

flowchart TB
    subgraph Client
        GUI["GUI"] -->|actions|Coord["Client coordination"]
        Coord -->|scenes and sound events|GUI
        Coord <-->|messages|ClientNet["Networking"]
    end
    subgraph Server
        ServerNet["Networking"] <-->|inputs and state|Logic["Game logic"]
    end
    ClientNet <-->|UDP|ServerNet

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
The networking layer is split between the generic UDP transport and the R-Type protocol. rtype_network contains the socket, session, acknowledgement, and timeout logic without any gameplay knowledge. rtype_protocol owns the message definitions and binary serializers used on the wire; game code never reads raw packet bytes directly. Both NetworkServer and NetworkClient inherit from NetworkHost, and each runs a single network thread driven by an asio::io_context. The game loop only interacts with them through a thread-safe incoming event queue and an outgoing message queue.

This structure keeps the transport state machine and socket I/O off the main simulation thread. NetworkHost owns the UDP socket and the periodic tick timer, receives datagrams as they arrive, and dispatches them to NetworkServer or NetworkClient. In turn, those classes decide whether to accept a session, reject a handshake, queue a reliable message, or forward incoming game data to the rest of the project. See protocol.md and network-client.md.

NetworkHost also owns the two thread-safe queues used by the game thread: one for incoming NetworkEvents and one for outbound OutgoingMessages. The network thread drains the outgoing queue and flushes packets on a 10 ms tick, while the game thread drains events with poll() and sends commands with send() or broadcast(). The generic packet framing helpers are PacketHeader, PacketCodec, and the byte reader/writer pair, which handle endianness and bounds checks before the game layer sees any payload.

The class diagram below shows shared transport ownership: both endpoints inherit from NetworkHost, while each active connection tracks reliability state. Queues connect the network and game threads.

classDiagram
    class NetworkHost {
        <<abstract>>
        +start(port)
        +stop()
        +poll()
        #onDatagram()
        #sendMessage()
        #onTick()
    }
    class NetworkServer {
        +send(peer, type, payload, reliable)
        +broadcast(type, payload, reliable)
        +kick(peer)
    }
    class NetworkClient {
        +connect(host, port, name)
        +disconnect()
        +send(type, payload, reliable)
        +state()
    }
    class Connection {
        sequence and ack tracking
        reliable messages
        heartbeat and timeout
    }
    class UdpSocket
    class ThreadSafeQueue
    NetworkHost <|-- NetworkServer
    NetworkHost <|-- NetworkClient
    NetworkHost *-- UdpSocket
    NetworkHost *-- ThreadSafeQueue : incoming events, outgoing messages
    NetworkServer o-- Connection : one per client session
    NetworkClient *-- Connection

The following flow separates threads: outgoing commands are drained by the network tick, while incoming events wait in a queue until the game loop polls. The game loop does not perform socket I/O directly.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Game[Game thread]
        Loop[game loop]
    end
    subgraph Net[Network thread: io_context.run]
        Recv[async receive] --> Dgram[onDatagram]
        Tick[10 ms timer] --> Send[sendMessage then onTick flush]
    end
    Loop -- send, broadcast --> Out[(outgoing queue)]
    Out --> Tick
    Dgram --> In[(incoming event queue)]
    In -- poll --> Loop

One sentence on helpers: PacketHeader defines the 16-byte UDP header, PacketCodec frames messages into a datagram, and ByteWriter / ByteReader serialize big-endian values with bounds checks.

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
The presentation subsystem lives in gui/, behind IGui and native-independent types in GuiTypes.hpp. Client coordination decodes server state and submits complete scenes and sound events. The GUI owns window management, rendering, resources, local input, audio and Settings without deciding gameplay results.

The client requests a 1920 x 1080 window. The native window preserves 16:9, and the GUI scales the logical world to fit while keeping HUD coordinates in window pixels. See GUI and client presentation for responsibilities, code locations, frame order and resource lifecycle, and the GUI how-to for practical integration.

docs.title: Ownership and lifecycle
docs.text:
Gui::open() attempts audio initialization unless GuiConfig::audioEnabled is false. An unavailable device leaves rendering and input operational. IGui::isAudioAvailable() reports whether this GUI owns a ready audio device.

AudioSystem exclusively owns the device it opens. It refuses to take over an already initialized external device. Other code must not close its device. On shutdown, playback voices are stopped and unloaded before their shared source sounds; the audio device is closed last. Repeated shutdown calls are safe.

docs.title: Load effects
docs.text:
Load effects after opening the GUI:

if (gui.isAudioAvailable() &&
    !gui.audio().loadSound("shot", "audio/demo-shot.wav")) {
    std::cerr << gui.audio().getLastError() << '\n';
}

Paths use the same asset root as visual resources, independent of the working directory. Sound IDs have their own namespace. Repeating an ID and normalized path reuses the sound; assigning that ID another path fails.

Missing, empty, invalid or unsupported files and native buffer creation failures return false and populate getLastError(). Failed loads are not cached. The caller can report the problem and continue without that effect.

docs.title: Trigger effects
docs.text:
const std::array<rtype::gui::SoundEvent, 1> events{{{"shot"}}};
gui.playAudio(events);

The client supplies events when they occur. The GUI does not infer gameplay events from rendering data. Unknown sound IDs are skipped and recorded in the audio manager's last error. Playback is a no-op when audio is unavailable.

Each loaded effect has eight playback voices sharing its sample data. Repeated events can overlap, including multiple instances of the same effect. If all eight voices for an effect are playing, a new instance is dropped. Existing voices and other effects continue; no voice is stolen.

docs.title: Volume and mute
docs.text:
Players can adjust and save these values through Settings. The GUI defaults to 50% volume, unmuted.

gui.setAudioSettings({0.5F, false}); // Half volume
gui.setAudioSettings({0.5F, true});  // Mute

Settings can be applied before opening the GUI or during playback. Volume must be finite and between 0 and 1; invalid settings throw without changing the previous settings. Updates affect existing and future voices.

Muting sets existing voices to zero volume while their playback continues. New events are discarded while muted. Unmuting restores the configured volume. Saved preferences are loaded on opening. Explicit API audio settings override the saved audio values; use Apply and save to persist session changes.

docs.title: Current client integration
docs.text:
After opening the GUI, the client loads the two existing generated test effects: audio/demo-shot.wav as shot and audio/demo-hit.wav as hit. These are placeholder tones, not a final sound pack. No new audio assets are required.

The client decodes GameEvent messages from the server and maps them as follows:

Server event Sound ID Shoot shot Hit hit Kill hit PlayerDeath hit

Sounds are triggered by received server events, including other players and enemies, rather than local keyboard presses. The client does not display event notices. Muting or disabling audio currently has no equivalent event text.

Events received while Settings or a connection status page is displayed are not played or queued for later. Network and world updates continue. Voices already playing may finish. Volume, mute and overlapping voices follow the AudioSystem rules above. Missing sound assets are logged and skipped without blocking gameplay or rendering.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Run a server and a connected client with an audio device available. Hold Fire and check that server-confirmed shots produce sound. Change volume, mute and unmute in Settings; apply each change. Check that mute and --no-audio suppress sound without affecting gameplay. Missing assets must not prevent movement or rendering.

The automated audio test replaces native audio calls with a fake backend to check initialization failures, loading, overlapping voices, volume, mute and cleanup ordering without a physical device. These checks do not confirm the new server-event playback on real hardware; that requires a manual check.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
Option Strengths Trade-offs Asio Cross-platform async I/O, stable event loop, header-only via CPM, no Boost dependency Adds a networking library to the build Raw sockets No external library, direct control of the stack Requires per-platform socket setup and more custom error handling TCP channel Simple stream API and built-in congestion control Head-of-line blocking causes input and snapshot delays under loss UDP + custom reliability Keeps gameplay traffic low latency and lets us choose which messages are reliable Requires an ack, resend and timeout layer to be implemented and tested

Choice: standalone Asio for the transport layer, with our own acknowledgement and timeout rules on top of UDP. TCP would hide loss behind head-of-line blocking and make every input update wait behind later packets, while raw sockets would require OS-specific socket initialization and a custom event loop. The game uses a single UDP socket per side and only marks the critical messages as reliable.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
Action Key Move up Up arrow Move down Down arrow Move left Left arrow Move right Right arrow Fire Space Open/close Settings F1 or Escape

The Settings button can also be clicked. Escape no longer closes the window. Use the close button or Quit application in Settings to exit.

Change gameplay bindings through Settings. Supported keys are arrows, Space, A to Z, Enter, and left/right Control and Shift.

docs.title: Action states
docs.text:
Call IGui::pollActions() once per frame before rendering. Raylib polls native window events at the end of rendering and exposes them on the next iteration.

Each PlayerActions array is indexed by PlayerAction:

  • heldActions: the action is currently held.
  • pressedActions: the action became held since the previous poll.
  • releasedActions: the action stopped being held since the previous poll.

Focus loss releases actions; unfocused input is ignored. Held keys are sampled again when focus returns. Settings releases gameplay actions while it is open. On startup, after API rebinding and after closing Settings, sampled keys must return to neutral before gameplay input resumes.

The GUI reports actions. Client/game systems own movement, firing behavior and network transmission.

docs.title: Programmatic bindings
docs.text:
Bindings use GuiKey without exposing native key codes.

rtype::gui::KeyBindings bindings;
bindings.keys[static_cast<std::size_t>(rtype::gui::PlayerAction::Fire)] =
    rtype::gui::GuiKey::F;
gui.setKeyBindings(bindings);

The setter replaces the complete binding set. GuiKey::None disables a binding. Multiple actions may share a key through the API; interactive rebinding swaps conflicting bindings. Invalid key values throw without changing the bindings.

See Settings for saving, restoring and local verification.

docs.text:
A component is plain data, defined in Components.hpp. Systems read and write components; components contain no logic.

Component Fields Meaning Position x, y Where the entity is. Velocity dx, dy Movement per second. Hitbox width, height Rectangle used for collisions. Health current, max Hit points. Hit amount Damage waiting to be applied. Not part of any archetype: added when needed. Damage value Damage dealt on contact. Lifetime remaining Seconds before the entity is removed. Invincibility remaining Seconds during which the entity cannot be hurt. Controllable up, down, left, right, shoot Current input state of a player ship. PlayerOwner playerId Which player owns the entity. The client picks the ship color or sprite from it. EnemyBehavior pattern, speed, amplitude, frequency How an enemy moves. pattern is Straight, Sine or Chase. Weapon cooldown, timer, projectileType, rate How and when the entity shoots. docs.title: 4. Archetypes (entity factory)
docs.text:
An archetype is a named list of components. EntityFactory builds the entity in one call, so component lists are written in one place only.

Component player enemy_basicenemy_sineenemy_chase player_missileenemy_missile explosion background Position ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Velocity ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Health ✓ ✓ Hitbox ✓ ✓ ✓ Damage ✓ ✓ Controllable ✓ PlayerOwner ✓ EnemyBehavior ✓ Weapon ✓ ✓ Score ✓ ✓ Invincibility ✓ Projectile ✓ Lifetime ✓ ✓ NetType ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓

Text description: the table lists, for each archetype, which components the factory adds. For example, player has ten components (everything except Damage, EnemyBehavior, Projectile and Lifetime), and explosion has only three: Position, Lifetime and NetType.

The factory decides which components an entity has. The caller decides their values through ComponentParams; a field that is not set keeps the default value of the component. The engine contains no gameplay numbers.

engine::EntityFactory factory(registry);

const Entity ship = factory.create("player", {
    .position = {150.F, 200.F},
    .health   = Health{3, 3},
    .hitbox   = Hitbox{64.F, 32.F},
    .playerId = 1,
});

Fields of ComponentParams must be written in their declaration order (a C++20 rule for designated initializers). An unknown name throws std::invalid_argument. The enemy pattern comes from the archetype name (enemy_sine gives Sine) unless .behavior is given.

docs.text:

EnemyBehavior, Velocity, Position WeaponSystem Handles cooldowns and creates missiles. Weapon, Controllable, Position MotionSystem Moves entities: position changes by velocity over time. Position, Velocity BoundsSystem Deals with entities that leave the play area (configured with an area and a margin). Position CollisionSystem Finds overlapping hitboxes and publishes CollisionEvent. Position, Hitbox DamageSystem Applies damage after a collision and publishes DamageEvent. Health, Damage, Invincibility DeathSystem Removes entities whose health reached zero and publishes EntityDiedEvent. Health LifetimeSystem Counts Lifetime down and removes the entity at zero. docs.title: 6. Execution order and event flow
docs.text:
Systems run in the order they are added with Update::addSystem. The order matters: a collision must be found before damage is applied.

Intended order of one step (1/60 s):

# Step System 1 Input InputSystem 2 Behavior EnemyBehaviorSystem 3 Weapons WeaponSystem 4 Motion MotionSystem, BoundsSystem 5 Collision CollisionSystem 6 Damage DamageSystem 7 Death DeathSystem 8 Cleanup LifetimeSystem, deferred destruction (flushDestroyed) 9 Spawn Waves of enemies (server game logic)

Registered today by ServerGame: InputSystem, MotionSystem, BoundsSystem. The other systems are added to the same list as they are connected.

flowchart LR
    Coll[CollisionSystem] -- CollisionEvent --> Dmg[DamageSystem]
    Dmg -- DamageEvent --> Death[DeathSystem]
    Death -- EntityDiedEvent --> After[Score, explosion,<br/>network message]
    Spawn[Spawning code] -- EntitySpawnedEvent --> Net[Network message]

Text description: events let systems react to each other without knowing each other. The collision system publishes a collision event, which the damage system reads. The damage system publishes a damage event, which the death system reads. The death system publishes an entity-died event, used for score, an explosion and the message sent to the clients. When an entity is spawned, an entity-spawned event is used to build the network message.

Rules that keep this predictable:

  • Events are queued with publish and delivered at one point of the step (EventDispatcher::flush), never in the middle of another system's loop.
  • Entities are removed with Registry::destroyLater and really destroyed with flushDestroyed at the end of the step, so no system iterates over a destroyed entity.
  • Systems count time with the step duration dt, never with frames.

docs.title: Evaluation criteria
docs.text:
We compare the options on the axes that matter for this project: decoupling of systems, performance with many short-lived entities (missiles), ease of replicating state over the network, multithreading, support for data-driven content, reusability (the engine must serve a second game) and implementation effort within the six-week timeframe.

The ratings in the architecture table (Excellent, Good, Medium, Poor) are a qualitative assessment by the team, based on the documentation and articles listed in the references. Performance statements come from the literature and the documentation of the technologies, not from benchmarks of our own.

docs.title: 1. Engine architecture
docs.text:
To build a modular, high-performance R-Type engine capable of handling multiple concurrent entities while synchronizing with an authoritative server, we evaluated several architectural patterns.

Criterion ECS OOP Inheritance Classic Component (Unity-like) Actor + Components (Unreal-like) Scene Graph (Godot-like) Actor Model (Messages) Manual DOD Principle Entities = IDs, components = data, systems = logic Class hierarchy Objects with components having an update() Actors + components with built-in replication Node tree Isolated units communicating via messages Arrays of structs by type Decoupling Excellent Poor Medium Good Poor Excellent Medium Performance (many missiles) Excellent Poor Medium Medium Poor Medium Excellent Network / Snapshots Simple (component replication) Difficult Medium Good (engine-bound) Difficult Natural (messages) Simple but non-generic Multithreading Good (independent systems) Difficult Difficult Difficult Difficult Natural Good Data-Driven Content Very good Poor Good Good Medium Medium Poor Reusability (engine + 2nd game) Excellent Poor Medium Medium Medium Good Very poor Simplicity / Timeframe Medium Excellent Good Poor Good Poor Good Verdict Chosen Too rigid Logic coupled to data Too heavy, engine-specific Unnecessary hierarchy for server Useful for instances, not entities Non-generic

Choice: ECS (Entity Component System).

Why: strict separation between data and logic, optimal performance with numerous simultaneous projectiles, and straightforward network state replication per component.

Limitations of ECS: - More indirection than plain objects: behavior is spread across systems, so following one feature means reading several files. - Debugging is less direct: there is no single object to inspect, only IDs and component pools. - The order of systems matters and must be defined explicitly (for example, collision before damage). - Relations between entities (a missile and its owner) must be stored as entity IDs, and checked with the generation counter.

Closest alternatives: - Classic component (Unity-like) keeps logic inside each component, which couples data and logic and makes replication harder. - Manual data-oriented design gives the same performance but would be written for R-Type only, which breaks the reusability requirement.

docs.title: 1.1 Writing our own ECS or using an existing library
docs.text:
Once ECS is chosen, there is a second question: do we write the core ourselves, or use an existing C++ ECS library such as EnTT or flecs?

Option Advantages Drawbacks Write our own core Full control over the design (server/client split, network IDs, event system); every team member understands the code; matches the subject, which asks for an engine of our own design; the engine can be delivered as a standalone project with no extra dependency More work in the first weeks; fewer features than a mature library; we must write the tests and benchmarks ourselves EnTT (sparse-set based, header-only) Mature and heavily tested; same storage model as our choice The team would learn the library instead of designing the engine; part of the engine architecture would be hidden behind a third-party API flecs (archetype based) Rich features (queries, relationships, tooling) Heavier and more complex; archetype model rejected for this project (see 2.1)

Choice: write our own small ECS core, using the same storage model as EnTT (sparse sets), and keep it behind a narrow interface (Registry, ISystem, Update).

Why: the subject asks for a game engine of our own design, and the Advanced Architecture track evaluates the quality of its abstractions and its reusability. The size of the core is small (entities, sparse sets, registry, fixed-step loop, event dispatcher, entity factory), so the cost is acceptable. Because the interface is narrow, replacing our core with a library later would not change the game code.

docs.title: 2. Algorithms & data structures
docs.text: For each topic: the options we considered, our choice, and why.

docs.title: 2.1 ECS component storage
docs.text:
Option Add / remove Iteration Complexity unordered_map<Entity, T> O(1) Slow (cache misses) Low Sparse array (vector<optional<T>>) O(1) Medium (holes) Low Sparse set (vector<T> dense + vector<size_t> sparse) O(1) Fast (contiguous) Medium Archetypes (one table per component combination) Costly (entity copied to another table) Fastest High

Choice: one sparse set per component type.

Why: missiles appear and disappear all the time, so adding and removing components must be cheap. A sparse set does that in O(1) and keeps data in a packed array, which is fast to iterate. Archetypes iterate slightly faster, but every component change moves the entity to another table, and the implementation is much heavier for this project. The iteration ratings come from the literature, not from our own measurements.

Entity IDs are an index plus a generation counter, so an old ID (for example in a late network packet) is detected as invalid instead of pointing to a new entity.

How a sparse set works, with three entities (2, 7 and 5) that have a position:

flowchart LR
    subgraph sparse["sparse (indexed by entity ID)"]
        s2["entity 2 → 0"]
        s7["entity 7 → 1"]
        s5["entity 5 → 2"]
    end
    subgraph dense["dense (components, no holes)"]
        d0["0: position of entity 2"]
        d1["1: position of entity 7"]
        d2["2: position of entity 5"]
    end
    s2 --> d0
    s7 --> d1
    s5 --> d2

Text description: the sparse array gives the position of an entity's component in the dense array, in O(1). Systems iterate over dense directly. To remove an entity, its slot is filled with the last element of dense, so there are never holes.

docs.title: 2.2 Collision detection
docs.text:
Option Cost Note All pairs O(n²) Too slow with many missiles Uniform grid O(n) Simple, rebuilt every tick Quadtree O(n log n) Overkill for similar-sized objects

Choice: uniform grid to find candidate pairs, then an AABB (rectangle) test.

Why: R-Type hitboxes are rectangles of similar size, so a grid is enough and easy to rebuild each tick. Fast missiles could skip over a target between two ticks, so we limit their speed per tick. Only the server decides the result of a collision (damage, death).

Limit: the cost is close to O(n) only when entities are spread roughly evenly over the cells. If many entities fall into the same cell (for example a crowd of enemies in one spot), that cell approaches the all-pairs cost. The cell size is configurable, so it can be tuned if this happens.

docs.title: 2.3 Game loop
docs.text:
Option Problem Variable timestep Result depends on CPU speed and frame rate Fixed timestep Needs a limit if the computer falls behind

Choice: fixed timestep of 1/60 s (60 updates per second), measured with std::chrono::steady_clock.

Why: - The game must not depend on CPU speed. With a fixed timestep, the same inputs give the same result on every machine. - Network reasoning is easier: everything is counted in updates. - On the client, drawing is separate from the simulation.

How it works: at each iteration, the real time that passed is added to a pending time. While the pending time is at least 1/60 s, the game runs one update and removes 1/60 s from it.

Limit: after a long freeze, making up all the lost time would take even longer. So the number of updates per iteration is capped, and the remaining time is dropped. The game slows down for a moment instead of freezing. In the code, the cap is Update::MaxCatchUpSteps (5 updates per iteration), and the clock can be replaced for tests.

flowchart TD
    A["New loop iteration"] --> B["Add the real time that passed to the pending time"]
    B --> C{"Pending time of at least one update,<br/>and maximum not reached ?"}
    C -- yes --> D["Run one update, remove 1/60 s of pending time"]
    D --> C
    C -- no --> E["Maximum reached ? Drop the remaining time"]
    E --> F["Draw the frame (client) or wait (server)"]
    F --> A

Text description: each iteration adds the real time that passed to the pending time. While there is at least one update of time, the game runs an update. When there is not enough time left, or the maximum is reached, the loop draws or waits, then starts again. If the maximum was reached, the extra time is dropped.

docs.title: 2.4 Communication between systems
docs.text:
Systems must react to each other (a collision leads to damage, damage to death, death to score) without knowing each other.

Option Advantages Drawbacks Direct calls between systems Simplest Systems depend on each other, which breaks decoupling and reuse Immediate callbacks (observer) Reaction happens at once Hard to follow; an entity can be destroyed in the middle of another system's loop Typed events in a queue, flushed at a defined point of the tick Systems only know the event types; the order of reactions is predictable; the events can also feed the network layer Reaction is delayed to the flush point; one more concept to learn

Choice: typed events sent to a queue, and flushed at a defined point of the tick.

Why: it keeps systems decoupled (a Mediator-style approach), and the order stays easy to reason about. The same events (entity spawned, entity died) are used to build network messages, so replication does not need a second mechanism. Together with deferred destruction at the end of the tick, it also avoids destroying an entity while a system is iterating over it.

docs.title: 2.5 Summary
docs.text: Topic Choice Engine architecture ECS, own core ECS storage Sparse set, index + generation IDs Collisions Uniform grid + AABB Game loop Fixed timestep with accumulator Randomness mt19937 per game, timer-driven spawn Communication between systems Typed events, flushed at a defined point of the tick

docs.title: 3. Decision and implementation consequences
docs.text:
We select an ECS with our own small core, sparse-set storage, a fixed-timestep loop, a uniform-grid collision system and typed events between systems.

We accept the limits listed in section 1 (indirection, harder debugging, explicit system order) and we reduce them with the rules below.

  • Keep the engine independent from the rest of the project: engine/ contains no networking or rendering code. It currently ships the components and archetypes of this game (for example Weapon, EnemyBehavior); for a second game, these game-specific parts would be moved out while the ECS core (entities, registry, sparse sets, loop, events) stays unchanged.
  • Keep gameplay values out of the engine: the entity factory decides which components an entity has, and the caller gives their values (health, speed, hitbox...) through ComponentParams.
  • Run one registry, one update loop and one event dispatcher per game instance, with no shared state between games.
  • Separate server code from client code: rendering, audio and input mapping live in gui/ and exist only on the client, and the server builds and runs without any graphics library.
  • Define the execution order of systems explicitly (input, behavior, weapons, motion, collision, damage, death, cleanup, spawn).
  • Destroy entities in one place, at the end of the tick, so no system iterates over a destroyed entity.
  • Store relations between entities as IDs with a generation counter, and reject stale IDs received from the network.
  • Keep the server authoritative: the client never decides collisions, damage or deaths.
  • Drive spawning, cooldowns and animations by game time, never by frames.
  • Revisit a choice if a problem shows up during development (for example a tick that exceeds its time budget).

docs.title: Graphics, audio and input library study
Requirements
docs.text: The GUI needs window management, 2D sprites, animation frames, scrolling backgrounds, text, keyboard input and sound effects. The library must integrate with C++ and CMake, support Linux and Windows, and remain isolated from networking and game logic.

docs.title: Evaluation criteria
docs.text: We compare functionality, API design, resource management, integration effort, platform support, documentation and measured performance. Integration effort is a qualitative assessment, not a measurement of development time.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
The evaluated versions are raylib 5.5, SFML 3.0.2 and SDL 3.2.8. These are evaluation baselines, not necessarily the latest releases.

Criterion raylib SFML SDL3 API C functions and structures C++ classes C functions and handles 2D rendering Texture and shape drawing Sprite, texture and shape classes Texture rendering Keyboard input Key state queries Events and key state queries Events and keyboard state queries Text Built-in font loading and drawing Font and text classes SDL_ttf or another text renderer Audio Sound loading and playback SoundBuffer and Sound classes Core audio API; SDL_mixer provides higher-level facilities Images Built-in loaders, depending on configuration Graphics module Core BMP loading; SDL_image extends format support Cleanup Explicit unload functions Resource-owning C++ objects Explicit destroy functions Linux and Windows Supported upstream Supported upstream Supported upstream Documentation Cheatsheet and examples Tutorials and API reference API wiki and examples

Upstream platform support does not establish successful application testing on both platforms.

docs.title: raylib
docs.text: raylib provides rendering, input, fonts and audio within one library. Its explicit resource management requires C++ RAII wrappers. Resources must be released exactly once, including when initialization fails. Graphics resources must be released before closing the window; sounds must be released before closing the audio device. System dependencies and enabled asset formats still require build configuration.

docs.title: SFML
docs.text: SFML provides graphics, window and audio modules through a native C++ API. Resource-owning objects simplify cleanup. Textures must still outlive sprites that reference them, and sound buffers must outlive sounds that use them.

docs.title: SDL3
docs.text: The comparison uses core SDL3 with BMP images and WAV audio. SDL_image, SDL_ttf and SDL_mixer can provide additional image formats, text rendering and higher-level audio operations. Those extensions add dependencies and configuration. Resource handles require explicit cleanup through appropriate C++ wrappers.

docs.title: Prototype evaluation
docs.text: The comparison prototype uses a shared scene with enemies, one player and 24 projectiles. Its adapters implement rendering, keyboard input and a short sound effect. Benchmark results measure frame throughput; they do not independently validate audio correctness, complete input behavior or Windows compatibility.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
Setting Value Operating system Linux, kernel 6.8.0-146-generic Architecture x86_64 Resolution 1280 x 720 Enemy counts 100, 1,000 and 5,000 Measurement duration 15 seconds Warm-up 2 seconds Repetitions Three per library and enemy count VSync Requested off V2 configuration HUD and audio disabled; fixed ship animation frame

The measured loop includes input, simulation, rendering and presentation. Initialization and resource loading are excluded.

docs.title: V2 results
docs.text:
Each value is the median of three per-run measurements. The p95 row summarizes per-run p95 values, not pooled frame samples.

Metric SFML SDL3 raylib 100 enemies, FPS 662.6 712.3 715.9 1,000 enemies, FPS 488.4 555.8 575.0 5,000 enemies, FPS 243.2 272.6 438.7 5,000 enemies, mean frame duration 4.112 ms 3.669 ms 2.279 ms 5,000 enemies, p95 frame duration 12.694 ms 13.441 ms 12.278 ms

docs.text:
GPU model, driver, power mode, compiler and optimization flags were not recorded. The adapters do not enforce identical GPU batching, and no separate GPU timing was measured. V2 excludes audio playback, HUD drawing and changing animation frames. The scene is not a complete multiplayer game.

The earlier V1 results differ substantially:

Metric SFML SDL3 raylib 5,000 enemies, median FPS 390.4 438.0 452.1 5,000 enemies, median per-run p95 3.621 ms 3.412 ms 4.416 ms

Missing environment information prevents a reliable explanation of the V1/V2 variation. These results support a local evaluation, not a universal ranking. The tables summarize two local benchmark sessions. Their recorded conditions and measurement limitations are detailed above. The prototype source code is not included here.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
We select raylib for rendering, audio and input.

Our qualitative assessment favors its direct multimedia API and the ability to cover the required features through one library. C++ wrappers will keep library-specific types and resource management inside gui/.

Measured rendering throughput supports this choice for the evaluated scene. It does not establish that raylib is always faster or easier to use.

We accept responsibility for explicit resource cleanup, build configuration and platform-specific integration. SFML remains a credible alternative for native C++ resource objects. SDL3 remains a credible alternative for lower-level control and a custom combination of multimedia facilities.

docs.title: Implementation consequences
docs.text:
• Integrate raylib through the existing dependency management workflow.
  • Keep raylib types out of public client and shared game interfaces.
  • Encapsulate window, rendering, resources, input and audio operations.
  • Make resource-owning wrappers non-copyable.
  • Report loading failures and unknown resource IDs.
  • Validate production builds and runtime behavior on Linux and Windows.
  • Complete functional checks for input, audio and resource cleanup.
  • Revisit the choice if representative gameplay reveals a limitation.

docs.title: GUI and client presentation
docs.text: The client converts server state into presentation data. The GUI displays that data, samples local input and owns the window, resources, audio and Settings. It does not decode network packets or decide movement, damage or scores.

docs.title: Responsibilities and code locations
docs.text:
Paths below are relative to the repository root.

Area Location Responsibility Client coordination client/src/main.cpp, ClientNetwork.hpp, ClientWorld.hpp Decode server events, maintain visible entities and player names, send inputs, build scenes and sound events. Public GUI contract gui/src/IGui.hpp, gui/include/GuiTypes.hpp Define lifecycle, action states, scenes, status feedback, preferences and sound events without native dependency types. Window and rendering gui/src/Gui.cpp, Window.cpp, Renderer.cpp, ScrollingBackground.cpp, StatusPresenter.cpp Manage the frame, window, world scaling, draw order, starfield and status pages. Visual resources gui/src/ResourceManager.cpp, gui/src/detail/ResourceManagerData.hpp Own native textures and fonts and resolve IDs used in scene data. Input and preferences gui/src/InputReader.cpp, InputMapper.cpp, SettingsMenu.cpp, SettingsStore.cpp Read keyboard/mouse state, map actions, edit preferences and persist applied settings. Audio gui/src/AudioSystem.cpp Own the device, sound resources and overlapping playback voices.

Native raylib types stay in implementation files and the private resource data header. detail/ contains implementation data shared by the resource manager and renderer; it is not part of the client contract. GLFW calls for the native aspect-ratio constraint stay in Window.cpp. The project uses raylib's bundled GLFW headers and symbols rather than installing a second GLFW library.

IGui is sufficient for frame processing. Concrete Gui::resources() and Gui::audio() provide resource registration and error reporting before use.

docs.title: Frame flow
docs.text:
1. Call pollActions() once to obtain held, pressed and released actions.
  2. Drain network events on the client thread and update ClientWorld and names.
  3. Convert server gameplay events into SoundEvent values and call playAudio().
  4. Serialize held actions into an InputMessage while connected.
  5. Build the current RenderScene, including connection feedback, and call render() even when Settings or a status page is visible.

These are the steps used in client/src/main.cpp. Network transport runs on its own thread; scene construction and native GUI calls remain on the client thread. Opening Settings releases gameplay actions without stopping network updates. Native input events collected by rendering are sampled on the next iteration.

See use the GUI for a minimal consumer and controls for input transitions and rebinding.

docs.title: Presentation data
docs.text:
Data Meaning SpriteDraw Texture ID, source region, destination rectangle, origin, rotation, tint, layer and entity identifier. sceneTexts Text attached to the game world, such as player names. overlayTexts Text in window pixels, such as the title and FPS counter. worldSize Logical world dimensions; {0, 0} keeps pixel coordinates. background Whether the starfield is enabled, its color and scrolling speed. feedback None, Connecting, Rejected, Disconnected or Error, with a message. SoundEvent ID of a sound previously registered through AudioSystem.

The renderer retains no entities between frames. Submit an entity every frame while it should be visible; omitting it removes it immediately. The client keeps network entity IDs in GuiEntityId::index and uses generation zero because the current wire IDs identify entities for the lifetime of the game.

Sprites use top-left destination coordinates. Server positions are entity centers, so main.cpp subtracts half the sprite's width and height when building the destination rectangle. Player types select sprite variants; connected and joined-player messages provide the labels. Until a name is known, the label is Player.

docs.title: Window, coordinates and draw order
docs.text:
The current client requests 1920 x 1080. Window applies a minimum of 640 x 360 and configures the resizable native window to preserve 16:9 once at creation. It does not call SetWindowSize() every frame. Escape is reserved for Settings; use the close button or Quit application to exit.

With worldSize = {1920, 1080}, Gui uniformly scales sprite destinations, origins and scene text to fit the current window and centers the result. Source texture regions remain unchanged. Overlay positions remain in window pixels. The player's text-size preference is applied on top of world scaling for scene text and directly to HUD text. Client HUD positions must allow larger fonts.

The world rendering order is:

  1. Clear color and starfield.
  2. Sprites in ascending layer order, preserving submission order within a layer.
  3. Scene text.
  4. Optional full-window scene tint.
  5. UI rectangles, then overlay text, including the Settings button.

Settings replaces the game view when open. Otherwise, non-None status feedback replaces it with a readable status page. Neither case stops the client loop. The starfield uses elapsed frame time for scrolling. The HUD FPS count is an average refreshed approximately twice per second, separate from the FPS target.

docs.title: Resource and audio lifecycle
docs.text:
Open the GUI before loading textures, fonts or sound effects. Resource IDs are independent of filenames. Visual loading errors throw; audio loading failures return false with getLastError(). Report the error before continuing.

Gui::close() closes audio, clears visual resources and then closes the window. Do not close the graphics context while resources using it remain alive. A standalone resource manager must be cleared or destroyed first.

The client currently maps server Shoot events to shot and Hit, Kill and PlayerDeath to hit. It uses the two generated placeholder WAV files already in assets/audio/. No action text is displayed. See audio for mute, voice limits and behavior while Settings is open, and add a GUI resource for registration examples.

docs.title: Preferences and validation
docs.text:
The GUI owns local keyboard, audio and visual preferences. Apply and save is the persistence boundary; Back discards unapplied edits. See Settings for paths, supported values and failure handling, and accessibility for current features and limitations.

Automated GUI tests run without a physical window or audio device. They cover the interface, resource errors, input mapping, Settings, status layouts, starfield motion, rendering order and native aspect-ratio configuration through fake boundaries. They cannot establish hardware readability, audio quality or successful multiplayer rendering on Linux and Windows; those need manual checks.

docs.title: Network client
docs.text: The project now includes an event-driven UDP client wrapper for the authoritative server model used by R-Type. The implementation lives in the network layer and is validated by loopback and failure tests.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
NetworkClient is responsible for:

  • opening a UDP connection to a server
  • tracking the connection state machine
  • sending reliable and unreliable messages
  • receiving datagrams, validating headers, and decoding payloads
  • emitting structured events for connection success, disconnection and errors

The public API is defined around a small event model:

  • Connected
  • Disconnected
  • MessageReceived
  • ConnectionFailed

The event variant is declared in network/include/NetworkEvent.hpp.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Connection defaults are centralized in network/include/NetworkConfig.hpp. Those constants cover the default host, port, timeout values, and connection retry policy used by the client implementation.

Typical configuration values include:

  • default server address and port
  • maximum connect attempts
  • disconnect timeout
  • heartbeat cadence used during the connection lifecycle

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
A client follows this lifecycle:

  1. Construct a NetworkClient with optional ClientConfig.
  2. Call connect(host, port, name).
  3. Wait for Connected or ConnectionFailed.
  4. Send messages through send(...) while in the connected state.
  5. Call disconnect() when the session ends.

The client exposes its current status via state(), which reports whether it is disconnected, connecting, connected or in a failing state.

docs.title: Sending and receiving data
docs.text:
The client serializes outgoing packets with the same binary protocol used by the server. It supports:

  • reliable messages for important state transitions
  • unreliable messages for frequent inputs and periodic updates
  • header validation and payload decoding before passing events to the caller

The network layer keeps the protocol parsing and transport concerns separate from the game logic, which makes the client easy to test against a loopback server.

docs.title: Failure handling
docs.text:
The client distinguishes between a clean disconnect and a connection failure. A failed attempt emits ConnectionFailed, including the reason, such as:

  • timeout while waiting for server acceptance
  • rejected connection
  • invalid protocol version
  • server already full
  • disconnect during the handshake

This behavior is covered by the network client test suite.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
The repository includes loopback tests for the client in tests/network_client_test.cpp. They validate:

  • successful connection against a real local server
  • failure when the server is unavailable or rejects the client
  • timeout and disconnect handling during connection setup

These tests are registered in tests/CMakeLists.txt and run as part of the project test suite.

docs.title: R-Type network protocol
docs.text:
Written so that someone could implement a new client from this document alone.

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD and MAY are used as in RFC 2119.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
• Transport: UDP. One socket per side, all traffic (connection, inputs, world updates, events) goes through it. The server listens on a port given on its command line.
  • Model: the server is authoritative. Clients send their inputs; the server simulates the game and sends back what happened.
  • Byte order: big-endian (network byte order) for every multi-byte field. Implementations MUST encode and decode field by field; copying a C/C++ struct to or from the wire is not allowed (padding and host byte order would leak into the format).
  • Versioning: every packet carries a version byte, currently 1. Any change to the packet layout or to an existing message increments it. A server MUST refuse a connection whose version differs from its own and MUST drop other packets with a wrong version.
  • Maximum datagram size: 1200 bytes, header included. This stays below common internet MTUs so packets are never fragmented. Senders MUST NOT exceed it; receivers MUST drop larger datagrams.
  • Client implementation: the repository also ships a NetworkClient wrapper around this protocol. It manages the connection state machine, emits Connected / Disconnected / ConnectionFailed events, and is validated by loopback tests against a local server.

docs.title: 1.1 Data types
docs.text:
Type Size Encoding u8 / u16 / u32 1 / 2 / 4 Unsigned integer, big-endian. i16 / i32 2 / 4 Signed integer, two's complement, big-endian. bool 1 0 or 1. Any other value makes the message invalid. string 1 + n u8 length n, then n bytes of UTF-8. No terminator. fixed 4 i32 in Q24.8: the value multiplied by 256. Used for positions (world units). fixed16 2 i16 in Q8.8: the value multiplied by 256. Used for velocities (world units per tick).

Floating-point numbers are never sent.

docs.title: 1.2 Repository layout for the protocol implementation
docs.text:
The current implementation in this repository is organized around the following files:

  • network/protocol/include/Fixed.hpp: fixed-point helpers for Q24.8 and Q8.8 values used in coordinates and velocities.
  • network/protocol/include/MessageType.hpp: enum values for the message IDs used by the protocol.
  • network/protocol/src/Messages.hpp: declarations for the game message payload types and validation helpers.
  • network/protocol/src/Messages.cpp: serialization, deserialization and validation logic for each message.
  • network/protocol/CMakeLists.txt: builds the protocol module in the project.
  • tests/protocol_messages_test.cpp: round-trip and rejection tests covering the message layout and invalid inputs.

The generic UDP transport layer lives in network/include and network/src; the protocol module above is the R-Type message layer used by that transport. The file list above matches the current repository layout and is kept in sync with the implementation.

docs.title: 2. Packet header
docs.text:
Every datagram starts with this 16-byte header, followed by zero or more messages until the end of the datagram.

Offset Size Field Description 0 2 magic Always 0x5254 (ASCII "RT"). 2 1 version Protocol version, 1. 3 1 flags Reserved. MUST be 0. 4 4 session Session token received in CONNECT_ACCEPT. 0 in CONNECT_REQUEST. 8 2 sequence Sequence number of this packet, incremented by the sender for every packet, wraps from 65535 to 0. 10 2 ack Most recent sequence received from the peer. 12 4 ackBits Bit n set means packet ack - 1 - n was also received (covers the 32 packets before ack).

docs.title: 2.1 Message framing
docs.text:
After the header, the datagram holds messages back to back:

Size Field Description 1 type Message type (§3). 1 channel 0 unreliable, 1 reliable. Any other value: invalid. 2 reliableId Present only when channel is 1. Identifies the message for deduplication; incremented by the sender for every new reliable message, wraps at 65535. 2 length Payload size in bytes. length payload Layout depends on type (§3).

docs.title: 2.2 Sequence numbers
docs.text:
Sequence numbers and reliable IDs wrap around. a is more recent than b when (int16)(a - b) > 0, computed on 16 bits. A plain a > b comparison is wrong after a wrap.

The implementation MUST use a wrap-safe comparison helper for 16-bit sequence values, for example:

  • sequenceGreater(a, b) returns true when a is newer than b across the 0..65535 rollover boundary.
  • 0 and 65535 are adjacent on wrap; a packet with sequence 0 is considered newer than one with sequence 65535 when compared in the correct modulo-16-bit order.

This rule is used for packet ordering and duplicate detection, and it is covered by unit tests for the rollover boundary.

docs.title: 2.3 Acknowledgements and reliability
docs.text:
• There is no separate ACK message: each side acknowledges what it received through ack / ackBits in the header of its next packet. A side with nothing else to send SHOULD send a packet with no messages within 100 ms so acknowledgements keep flowing.
  • The current implementation does not send this as a dedicated empty datagram on a fixed 100 ms timer. The client sends a lightweight packet on the next 10 ms network tick when it has nothing else to send; the server only acknowledges in the next outgoing packet (for example, a snapshot or a heartbeat after the 1 second idle period).
  • Unreliable messages are sent once. Losing one is harmless because a newer one replaces it (INPUT, SNAPSHOT, PING).
  • Reliable messages are kept by the sender and copied into new packets until a packet containing them is acknowledged. If one stays unacknowledged for 5 seconds, the sender considers the peer disconnected.
  • The receiver MUST process each reliableId only once and drop repeats.
  • Reliable messages are not guaranteed to arrive in order. A client receiving a SNAPSHOT entry or ENTITY_DESTROY for an entity it doesn't know yet MUST ignore it.
  • Because entityIds are never reused, a client SHOULD remember recently destroyed IDs and ignore an ENTITY_SPAWN that arrives after the matching ENTITY_DESTROY.

docs.title: 3. Messages
docs.text:
Types 0x01–0x0F are connection messages, 0x10 and up are game messages. Unknown types make the datagram invalid (§5).

Every payload MUST be exactly length bytes: a payload that is too short or has bytes left over is invalid.

docs.title: 0x01 CONNECT_REQUEST (unreliable, resent by the client, see §4)
docs.text:
Field Type Description name string Player name, 1 to 32 bytes.

Sent with session = 0.

docs.title: 0x04 DISCONNECT (reliable)
docs.text: Field Type Description reason u8 0 quit (also used when the server shuts down), 1 timed out, 2 kicked. Any unknown value is treated as quit by the client.

docs.title: 0x05 PING (unreliable)
docs.text:
Field Type Description timestamp u32 Sender's clock in milliseconds. A receiver SHOULD answer with PONG.

A receiver SHOULD answer with PONG. In the current implementation, the client does so for server PINGs, but the server currently ignores PING and does not yet send PONG, so server-side round-trip timing is not implemented yet.

docs.title: 0x06 PONG (unreliable)
docs.text: Field Type Description timestamp u32 The timestamp of the PING being answered.

docs.title: 0x10 INPUT (unreliable, every client tick)
docs.text:
Field Type Description clientTick u32 Client tick counter, increasing. The server ignores inputs older than the last one it applied. buttons u8 Bit 0 up, bit 1 down, bit 2 left, bit 3 right, bit 4 shoot. Bits 5–7 MUST be 0.

The client sends the current state of its controls, not key presses. A lost INPUT is replaced by the next one.

docs.title: 3.2 Server → Client
docs.text: DISCONNECT, PING and PONG are also sent by the server, with the same layout as in §3.1. A server DISCONNECT uses reason 0 for quit (also used when the server shuts down), 1 for timeout and 2 for kicked. A client treats any unknown value as quit.

docs.title: 0x02 CONNECT_ACCEPT (reliable)
docs.text: Field Type Description clientId u8 Identifier of this player for the rest of the game. sessionToken u32 Random, non-zero. The client MUST put it in the session field of every later packet. tickRate u8 Server simulation rate in ticks per second.

docs.title: 0x03 CONNECT_REJECT (unreliable)
docs.text: Field Type Description reason u8 1 server full, 2 version mismatch, 3 banned.

docs.title: 0x11 PLAYER_JOINED (reliable)
docs.text: Field Type Description clientId u8 The player who joined. name string Their name.

docs.title: 0x12 PLAYER_LEFT (reliable)
docs.text: Field Type Description clientId u8 The player who left. reason u8 0 quit, 1 timed out (crash or network loss), 2 kicked.

docs.title: 0x13 ENTITY_SPAWN (reliable)
docs.text:
Field Type Description entityId u32 Unique for the lifetime of the game. entityType u16 Kind of entity (player ship, enemy type, missile…), see the game's entity list. x, y fixed, fixed Initial position. entityType Entity 1–4 Player ship, owned by the client with that clientId 10 Basic enemy 20 Player missile 21 Enemy missile

World: 1920 × 1080 units, (0, 0) top-left, x/y are the centre of the entity. Snapshot velocities are in units per server tick (1/60 s).

docs.title: 0x14 ENTITY_DESTROY (reliable)
docs.text: Field Type Description entityId u32 Entity to remove. cause u8 0 left the screen, 1 killed, 2 other.

docs.title: 0x15 SNAPSHOT (unreliable, about 20 per second)
docs.text:
Field Type Description serverTick u32 Server tick of this snapshot. A client MUST ignore a snapshot older than the last one it applied. count u16 Number of entries that follow. entries count × 16 bytes Each: entityId u32, x fixed, y fixed, vx fixed16, vy fixed16.

count MUST match the payload size exactly (6 + 16 × count bytes). If the world doesn't fit in one datagram, the server sends several SNAPSHOT messages with the same serverTick.

docs.title: 0x16 GAME_EVENT (reliable)
docs.text: Field Type Description event u8 0 shoot, 1 hit, 2 kill, 3 player death. sourceId u32 Entity causing the event. targetId u32 Entity affected, or 0 if none.

docs.title: 4. Connection lifecycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: CONNECT_REQUEST(name), session = 0
    Note over C: resent every 500 ms, gives up after 10 tries
    alt accepted
        S-->>C: CONNECT_ACCEPT(clientId, sessionToken, tickRate)
        S-->>C: ENTITY_SPAWN for every existing entity
        S--)C: PLAYER_JOINED (to the other players)
    else refused
        S-->>C: CONNECT_REJECT(reason)
    end
    loop while connected
        C->>S: INPUT, every client tick
        S-->>C: SNAPSHOT, about 20 per second
        S-->>C: ENTITY_SPAWN / ENTITY_DESTROY / GAME_EVENT as they happen
    end
    C->>S: DISCONNECT(quit)
    S--)C: PLAYER_LEFT(quit) (to the other players)
    Note over S: no packet from a client for 5 s
    S--)C: PLAYER_LEFT(timed out) (to the other players)
  1. Connecting. The client sends CONNECT_REQUEST with session = 0 and repeats it every 500 ms until it gets an answer, up to 10 times. A server receiving a repeated CONNECT_REQUEST from an already accepted endpoint ignores it; the reliable CONNECT_ACCEPT is resent on the normal reliability resend cadence until the client acknowledges it.
  2. Session. After CONNECT_ACCEPT, every packet in both directions carries the sessionToken. The server identifies a client by its address, port and token; packets that don't match an existing session are dropped. This prevents someone from injecting packets for another player by faking their address.
  3. Keep-alive. A side that has sent nothing for 1 second SHOULD send a PING. The client does this; the server currently ignores PING and does not yet send PONG, so server-side round-trip time is not measured yet.
  4. Leaving. A client that quits sends DISCONNECT and stops after it is acknowledged or after 3 attempts. The server tells the other players with PLAYER_LEFT(quit).
  5. Timeout. If the server receives nothing from a client for 5 seconds (crash, network loss), it removes that client and sends PLAYER_LEFT(timed out) to the others. The game continues for the remaining players. A client that hears nothing from the server for 5 seconds considers itself disconnected.

docs.title: 5. Error handling
docs.text:
How malformed, truncated or oversized packets are handled.

The receiver checks each datagram in this order. The first failed check drops the whole datagram silently: no reply, no partial processing.

  1. Size below 16 bytes or above 1200 bytes.
  2. magic is not 0x5254, flags is not 0, or version is not 1. Exception: a CONNECT_REQUEST with a wrong version gets a CONNECT_REJECT(version mismatch) if the rest of it can be read.
  3. On the server: the sender is unknown and the first message is not CONNECT_REQUEST, or the sender is known but session doesn't match its token.
  4. A message header or payload runs past the end of the datagram, channel is not 0 or 1, or the message type is unknown. Message types below 0x10 are ignored by the transport layer if they are not recognized; message types at or above 0x10 are forwarded to the game layer, which validates them with the deserialization helpers from network/protocol.
  5. A payload doesn't decode to exactly length bytes, or a field is out of range: bool not 0/1, string empty or over 32 bytes, unknown enum value, reserved bits set, SNAPSHOT.count not matching the payload size.

The header decoder MUST reject these cases explicitly:

  • TooShort: data pointer is null or the datagram is shorter than the 16-byte header.
  • TooLong: the datagram is larger than 1200 bytes.
  • BadMagic: the first 2 bytes are not 0x5254.
  • BadVersion: the version byte is not 1.
  • BadFlags: the flags byte is not zero.

All header validation happens before any message payload is parsed, and all invalid packets are discarded without partial processing.

Implementation requirements:

  • Never trust a length or count field for allocation. Every size is checked against the bytes actually received before reading or reserving memory. One fixed 1200-byte receive buffer per socket is enough.
  • A malformed packet MUST NOT crash the program, throw an uncaught exception, or make memory grow.
  • The server SHOULD enforce a per-address packet rate limit, a pending-connection limit, and a disconnect path for clients that keep exceeding the limits. This is planned and tracked under issue #18.
  • Duplicate and out-of-date packets are normal on UDP and are not errors: they are handled by §2.2 and §2.3.

docs.title: Open the menu
docs.text:
Press F1 or Escape, or click the Settings button. The menu also remains available on connection status pages. Escape opens or closes Settings; use the window close button or Quit application to exit.

Use a window of at least 640 x 360.

Control Effect Up / Down Select a row Left / Right Change a value Enter or Space Activate the selected row Escape or F1 Back, or cancel key capture Mouse wheel Move the selection Click a row Activate it Click its left/right arrow Decrease/increase a value

Menu controls stay fixed when gameplay controls are rebound.

docs.title: Available settings
docs.text:
Setting Choices Default Volume 0 to 100%, steps of 5% 50% Mute On / Off Off Background motion On / Off On UI text size 100%, 125%, 150% 100% Scene tint Off, Red, Green, Blue, Amber Off Tint opacity 0 to 50%, steps of 5% 15% Keyboard bindings Movement and fire Arrows and Space

The tint is a full-window colored rectangle blended over the game scene. It covers the background, sprites and scene text. UI rectangles, overlay text, Settings and connection status pages remain un-tinted. It requires no image asset or shader. It is a visual preference; it is not a color-vision correction or a simulation of a color-vision deficiency.

Text size scales menu text, connection status text and the scene/overlay text submitted by the client. The GUI scales the font size and character spacing; overlay positions remain in window pixels. When RenderScene::worldSize is set, sprite destinations, origins and scene text are scaled to fit that world in the window; overlay text and Settings keep their screen-space layout. The client must choose suitable HUD positions and wrapping for larger text.

Disabling background motion freezes the starfield. It does not pause gameplay, stop network updates or hide entities.

docs.title: Rebind keys
docs.text:
Activate a Key row, then press the new key. The activating press is not captured as the replacement. If another action uses that key, the two bindings are exchanged. Press Left on a Key row to remove its binding. Escape or F1 cancels capture.

Supported keys are arrows, Space, A to Z, Enter, left/right Control and left/right Shift. Escape and F1 are reserved for menu navigation.

docs.title: Apply and cancel
docs.text:
Changes stay in a draft until Apply and save is selected. The menu previews its text size immediately. Apply updates the running GUI and writes preferences to disk; the menu stays open and reports the result. Back, Escape or F1 discards changes made since the last Apply.

Restore defaults resets the draft. Apply it to keep the defaults.

Opening Settings releases gameplay actions. On startup, after API rebinding, and after closing Settings, all sampled gameplay keys must be released before input resumes. This avoids an activation key becoming an unintended shot.

The client must continue calling pollActions() and render() every frame while Settings is open. The menu does not pause the client or a multiplayer session.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Settings are loaded when the GUI opens and saved only by Apply and save.

Platform Default file Linux with absolute XDG_CONFIG_HOME $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/rtype/settings.conf Linux otherwise $HOME/.config/rtype/settings.conf Windows %APPDATA%/RType/settings.conf

An explicit GuiConfig::settingsPath replaces the default location. The client exposes it through --settings path. If no default directory is available, settings still apply for the session and saving reports an error.

The version 1 text format stores volume, mute, background motion, text scale, tint mode/opacity and five keyboard bindings. Missing optional values use defaults, and unknown entries are ignored. Unsupported versions, duplicate entries, invalid values or files larger than 16 KiB are rejected without partially applying settings.

Saving writes a temporary sibling file before replacing the previous file. A write error leaves the existing destination in place where replacement failed; details are logged to the terminal. If saving fails, the new values still apply for the current session. Invalid files are not overwritten until the user explicitly selects Apply and save.

Explicit API calls to setKeyBindings() or setAudioSettings() before opening take precedence over the corresponding saved preferences. API updates are not automatically written to disk.

docs.title: Local checks
docs.text:
cmake --preset release
cmake --build --preset release
ctest --preset release
./r-type_client

To use a separate test file on Linux:

./r-type_client --settings /tmp/rtype-settings-check.conf

Without --connect, the client shows an empty background with Settings available. To check movement against the authoritative server, use two terminals:

./r-type_server 4242

./r-type_client --connect 127.0.0.1:4242 --name Player

Only server entities are rendered. No local fixture ships, projectiles or scheduled enemy removals are created. The client opens at 1920 x 1080. Its 1920 x 1080 world fits the current window with uniform scaling and centered placement, preserving its aspect ratio.

  1. Open and close Settings with F1, Escape and the mouse.
  2. Rebind an action, apply, close Settings and verify movement in the connected game.
  3. Assign an already used key and check that the bindings are exchanged.
  4. Hold Fire, open the menu and verify that gameplay actions are released. After closing, release the key before testing Fire again.
  5. While connected, fire and check server-confirmed shot sounds. Change volume and mute, apply, restart and verify the saved values. Mute and --no-audio must suppress sound without preventing movement or rendering.
  6. Disable background motion and check that the stars stop scrolling.
  7. Apply each tint and change its opacity. The scene changes color while Settings and overlay text remain readable.
  8. Set text size to 150% and resize. Check labels, footer messages and HUD text.
  9. Apply settings, restart and check that they are restored.
  10. Change a setting then Back. Reopen and check that the change was discarded.
  11. Connect to an unavailable port, wait for failure and verify Settings remains reachable.

Automated tests cover draft edits, binding swaps, persistence/error paths, menu transitions, text scaling and tint drawing order using fake native boundaries. These tests do not validate actual window rendering or audio hardware. Record manual results on supported platforms before merging.

docs.title: How-tos
docs.text:
• Use the GUI: build, connect, drive the presentation loop and consume actions
  • Add a GUI resource: textures, sprite regions, fonts and sound effects
  • Add a third-party dependency: register a library through CPM

For subsystem responsibilities and code locations, start with the GUI overview or the architecture.

docs.title: Add a third-party dependency
docs.text:
1. Add a CPMAddPackage call in cmake/Dependencies.cmake, pinned to a tag:
CPMAddPackage(
    NAME fmt
    GITHUB_REPOSITORY fmtlib/fmt
    GIT_TAG 11.0.2
)
  1. Link it to the target that needs it:
target_link_libraries(r-type_server PRIVATE fmt::fmt)

  1. Reconfigure (cmake --preset debug). The sources land in .cpm-cache/ and are reused by every build afterwards.

  2. Add the library and the reason for choosing it to docs/comparative-study.md.

Never copy a library's source into the repository, and never rely on a system-installed library (except low-level platform ones such as OpenGL or X11).

docs.title: Choose a path and an ID
docs.text:
Place the file in the appropriate assets/ directory. Existing categories include player/, enemy/, boss/, projectiles/, effects/ and audio/. Record the source and license in assets/README.md when adding new content.

Paths below are relative to the asset root beside the executable. Filename capitalization must match on Linux and Windows. A resource ID is a separate application name: moving a file requires updating its load path, while scene data may keep the same ID.

Open Gui before registering resources. Register once at startup, not on every frame. Texture, font and sound IDs have separate namespaces.

docs.title: Add a texture and a sprite
docs.text:
The following uses an existing asset so the coordinates are reproducible:

gui.resources().loadTexture("players", "player/ship-variants.gif");
const auto size = gui.resources().getTextureSize("players");

Inspect the sheet and choose a source region within its dimensions. Then add drawing data to the scene:

rtype::gui::SpriteDraw ship;
ship.entityId = {1, 0};
ship.textureId = "players";
ship.sourceRect = {{67.0F, 2.0F}, 32.0F, 15.0F};
ship.destinationRect = {{100.0F, 100.0F}, 96.0F, 45.0F};
ship.layer = 10;
scene.sprites.push_back(ship);

Destination position is the top-left corner when origin is zero. When positions come from the server, convert its center coordinates before submitting the sprite. Higher layers draw later; equal layers preserve submission order.

Repeat the sprite in every scene while it should remain visible. To animate a sheet, select different sourceRect regions over time; loading a GIF does not start an animation automatically. Texture regions must have positive dimensions and stay inside the sheet. The renderer rejects invalid or unknown resources before starting the frame.

docs.title: Add a custom font
docs.text:
Place a supported font file, for example at assets/fonts/hud.ttf, and register it after opening the GUI. This example path is a file to add, not a bundled font.

gui.resources().loadFont("hud", "fonts/hud.ttf", 32);

rtype::gui::TextDraw title;
title.fontId = "hud";
title.text = "R-Type";
title.position = {20.0F, 20.0F};
title.fontSize = 24.0F;
scene.overlayTexts.push_back(title);

An empty font ID uses raylib's borrowed default font. A custom load that falls back to that default is treated as a failure. The current font loader does not provide a custom Unicode glyph list, so verify the characters actually needed.

docs.title: Add a sound effect
docs.text:
Load the sound when audio is available, and retain whether registration worked:

bool shotLoaded = false;
if (gui.isAudioAvailable()) {
    shotLoaded = gui.audio().loadSound("shot", "audio/demo-shot.wav");
    if (!shotLoaded)
        std::cerr << gui.audio().getLastError() << '\n';
}

When a validated gameplay event arrives, queue its sound once:

if (shotLoaded)
    soundEvents.push_back({"shot"});

Call gui.playAudio(soundEvents) once per client frame, then discard the events before collecting the next frame. Do not replay a sound just because its entity remains visible. The current client skips new gameplay sounds while Settings or a connection status page is shown.

Use the existing GameEvent handler in client/src/main.cpp when changing sound mapping. For a new effect, add its file, choose an ID, register it, and select that ID for the corresponding event. The two current WAV files are generated placeholder tones. See audio for volume, mute and voice limits.

docs.title: Handle failures and verify
docs.text:
Texture and font registration throw exceptions containing the resource ID and resolved path. Repeating the same ID, normalized path and font size reuses the resource; conflicting registrations throw. Sound registration returns false with an error string for conflicts and loading failures. Failed loads are not cached.

Check the resource on Linux and Windows, at small and large window sizes and with 150% text size. For sounds, also check mute, overlapping events, a missing file and --no-audio. These are manual checks, not results already established by this guide.

Do not call native unload functions from the client. Gui::close() releases resources before closing their native contexts. See the GUI overview and Settings for related behavior.

docs.title: Build and run the existing client
docs.text:
Install the platform dependencies listed in the repository README first. Run commands from the repository root.

On Linux:

cmake --preset release
cmake --build --preset release
ctest --preset release

Start the server in one terminal:

./r-type_server 4242

Start a client in another terminal:

./r-type_client --connect 127.0.0.1:4242 --name Goldy

On Windows, use Developer PowerShell:

cmake --preset windows
cmake --build --preset windows
ctest --preset windows

Then start the executables in separate terminals:

.\r-type_server.exe 4242

.\r-type_client.exe --connect 127.0.0.1:4242 --name Goldy

Without --connect, the client shows a background and Settings, without creating local players or enemies. F1, Escape and the Settings button open the menu. See Settings for rebinding, volume, text size and saving.

The current client also accepts --settings path, --no-audio, --mute and --volume 0..1. --name selects the name sent during connection. The client reports connection failures and disconnections through status feedback.

docs.title: Write a GUI consumer
docs.text:
Link the consumer target to rtype::gui. The existing executable also links the network and protocol targets because it handles multiplayer messages. Keep raylib and GLFW includes out of the consumer.

The following complete example shows the presentation lifecycle using one existing sprite sheet. It illustrates API usage; the production client should continue to build its scene from server state.

#include "Gui.hpp"

int main()
{
    rtype::gui::Gui gui;
    rtype::gui::GuiConfig config;
    config.width = 1920;
    config.height = 1080;
    gui.open(config);
    gui.resources().loadTexture("players", "player/ship-variants.gif");

    rtype::gui::RenderScene scene;
    scene.worldSize = {1920.0F, 1080.0F};
    scene.background.enabled = true;

    rtype::gui::SpriteDraw ship;
    ship.entityId = {1, 0};
    ship.textureId = "players";
    ship.sourceRect = {{67.0F, 2.0F}, 32.0F, 15.0F};
    ship.destinationRect = {{100.0F, 100.0F}, 96.0F, 45.0F};
    scene.sprites.push_back(ship);

    rtype::gui::IGui& presentation = gui;
    while (!presentation.shouldClose()) {
        const auto actions = presentation.pollActions();
        (void)actions;
        // The client consumes actions and updates scene data here.
        presentation.render(scene);
    }
    presentation.close();
}

Submit a complete current scene each frame. Source rectangles select image pixels; destinations use world coordinates when worldSize is set. HUD text belongs in overlayTexts, while names and world labels belong in sceneTexts.

docs.title: Integrate client events
docs.text:
Use client/src/main.cpp as the concrete integration reference:

  1. Decode server messages in registered ClientNetwork handlers.
  2. Apply spawns, destruction and snapshots to ClientWorld; do not create unknown entities from a snapshot.
  3. Keep received player names separately from sprite selection.
  4. Convert validated server gameplay events into sound IDs registered during startup. Call playAudio() once with that frame's events.
  5. Send held actions through InputMessage::serialize() with an increasing client tick. Settings returns released/neutral actions while open.
  6. Supply connection status through RenderScene::feedback, and continue polling and rendering until the user quits.

Do not decide hits, deaths or score changes in the GUI. The server owns those results. See the module overview, protocol and audio reference.
